items.title: Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes 2
items.summary: Classification: Severe, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: 8.7, CVEs: CVE-2026-66784, Summary: A flaw was found in Submariner. In its default Pre-Shared Key (PSK) mode, all gateways within a broker set utilize the same PSK. An attacker, by knowing this shared PSK, can forge an Endpoint Custom Resource (CR) to impersonate another cluster's identity. This enables the attacker to establish an Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) tunnel under the false identity, leading to a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack on network traffic between clusters.

items.title: ARTEX leads to persistent ZQAgent backdoor
items.summary: Over the last few months, NVISO has responded to an increasing amount of intrusions leveraging adversary LLM tools such as ARTEX. Several industry peers have corroborated1 this increased activity, with LLM-driven tools excelling at exploitation and credential abuse. LLM-driven intrusions have to date maintained a relatively consistent attack-chain commonly permitting containment through the isolation of its initial-access vector and the subsequent extensive revocation of compromised and staged credentials. Amplified by the speed and noise of LLMs, these intrusions are often experienced as smash-and-grab operations, rarely resulting in long-lasting footholds beyond collected and staged credentials. However, as part of a recent incident response engagement, NVISO observed ARTEX deploying ZQAgent, a new backdoor providing its operator with a long-lasting foothold within the target environment. The usage of a persistent backdoor by LLM-driven tools deviates from their current autonomous nature and is instead believed to be the result of operator-specific instructions. The usage of LLMs is still rarely observed2 in traditional backdoor deployment operations, we see no reason that, over the near future, the usage of LLMs would not widely spread to these historically conventional operations.

items.title: pulp_python: pull-through caching fetches a client-supplied url with the remote's credentials
items.summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: 10.0, CVEs: CVE-2026-126984, Summary: A **server-side request forgery** flaw has been found in the get_remote_artifact_url() function in pulp_python/app/models.py of the pull-through caching feature in the **pulp_python** package. The function uses the redirect query parameter from the client request as the URL to download. A network attacker or user who can reach the content app of a Python distribution that has a remote can choose that URL. The content app downloads it and returns the response. When the remote has a username and password, the download sends those credentials to the host in the URL. When the remote policy is immediate, the default, or on_demand, the file is saved into the distribution's repository and later clients are served that file. The project name and version come from the file, and the filename comes from the request path. A filename the repository already stores is served from the stored file. See also: https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/CVE-2026-126984

See also: https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/CVE-2026-126984

items.title: SYS010 malware abuses browser management to spy on Gmail, Outlook
items.summary: A new version of the SYS01 infostealer malware delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management to force the installation of an extension that steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook emails. The ads lure Windows users into downloading free animated wallpapers that work as advertised but also deploy malware in the background during installation. The campaign targets Facebook and Meta business accounts and gives the operator access to recent Gmail and Outlook messages in Chrome, and the ability to permanently delete emails. Bitdefender Labs tracks the campaign as SYS010 and says the malware is likely a new version of the SYS01 infostealer, observed since at least 2022 in malvertising activity on Facebook. The name reflects the researchers' assessment that this variant represents a major improvement over its predecessor, leading them to tag it as version 2, represented in binary as 010. Researchers identified a malicious SYS010 ad on October 16 and found that the campaign was still ongoing, with hundreds of ads created. Company telemetry shows that requests to the threat actor’s servers came from several countries in Asia, Europe, North America, Africa, and South America. Meta Ad Library' transparency page shows that one advertisement alone reached 6,275 users in the European Union, targeting anyone above 18.

items.title: Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers
items.summary: Cyprus' growing security ties with Israel and its use as a staging ground for Western forces operating across the Middle East appear to be making the island an increasingly attractive target for Iranian cyber espionage. Volant Manticore is an early example of that interest. The previously undocumented advanced persistent threat (APT) group has been targeting organizations in Cyprus as part of what researchers at Check Point describe as an Iranian intelligence-gathering campaign focused on the island. Nation-State Strategic Intelligence Gathering on Cyprus Targets Its targets so far have included a Cyprus-based airline operating primarily between Cyprus and Israel, telecommunications providers, critical infrastructure organizations, and a suspected government entity with military connections. The selection of targets suggests an effort to gather intelligence on the island's government, infrastructure, and relationships with regional partners, the researchers said. Check Point has assessed with medium confidence that Volant Manticore is likely an offshoot of the Iranian threat group MuddyWater, tasked primarily with spying on Cypriot organizations on behalf of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). It is among the first known Iranian groups to have a dedicated focus on Cyprus, although it has recently expanded its targeting to organizations in Saudi Arabia, says Sergey Shykevich, director of threat intelligence at Check Point Software. "Cyprus' defense and energy ties with Israel and Greece, along with its role in Western military operations in the region, may help explain why it is a target for intelligence gathering," Shykevich says.

items.title: Wyoming uranium operation shuts down after cyberattack
items.summary: Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems. The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project. Peninsula Energy said it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected. "The company's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange. The notification went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing. Peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said.

items.title: Palo Alto Networks warns of Fragnesia flaw exploited in PAN-OS attacks
items.summary: Threat actors are chaining exploits for the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia vulnerabilities to target Palo Alto Networks devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet. PHP2Shell is the name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which allow unauthenticated attackers to run code remotely with the privileges of the PHP web worker. The Fragnesia vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-46300, is a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that lets a local attacker with low-privileges to escalate permissions to root level. An alert from CISA on October 28 warned that both security issues were being chained in attacks to deploy PHP webshells on vulnerable systems and execute commands as root. Around the same time, Dream Security researchers reported observing a campaign using the same chain, targeting servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including a U.S. government affiliate. Palo Alto Networks has confirmed in an advisory today that such attacks also target firewalls running PAN-OS. “Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” reads the security bulletin. The networking company says that all exploitation activity it observed involved PAN-OS devices that exposed their management interface to the public internet, which goes against its recommended ‘best practices.’

items.title: Hackers help themselves to 1Password's source code and customer data
items.summary: 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code. The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information. 1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata. The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said. Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected. 1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions.
